title: Deep Incentive Design with Differentiable Equilibrium Blocks
one_liner: Learn rules for multi-party decision problems by putting an equilibrium solver inside a trainable pipeline, so one system can shape many games toward preferred outcomes.
lead: This paper studies incentive design: choosing rewards, prices, or contract terms so that several decision-makers settle on a desirable final pattern of actions. The hard part is that the final pattern is not chosen directly by the designer. It emerges from how players respond to the designed rules. Deep incentive design handles that by inserting an equilibrium-solving block inside a trainable pipeline, so the outer designer can improve rules based on the outcomes those rules create.

paras: A designer may want workers to pick efficient schedules, buyers and sellers to agree on good contracts, or competing agents to settle on a stable allocation. Yet the designer does not set those final actions by hand. The designer only sets the surrounding rules, and then each player responds to those rules.

That makes optimization hard because the quality of one rule choice can only be known after the players react and settle on an equilibrium. The paper's goal is to make that reaction step part of one trainable pipeline because rule design can only learn from outcome feedback when player responses are explicitly computed.

callout.html: Put an equilibrium solver inside the learning loop, because incentive design is really a two-level problem: choose rules, then watch how players respond to those rules.

panels.title: 1. The designer picks rules
panels.viz_args: contract terms, prices, or scheduling rewards
panels.caption: The designer chooses incentives, not the final player actions.

panels.title: 2. Players respond
panels.caption: Each player chooses actions that are best for them under the current rule choice.

panels.title: 3. An equilibrium block solves the game
panels.caption: The block returns the player behavior that is stable under those incentives.

panels.title: 4. Judge the outcome
panels.viz_args: compare the resulting behavior with the designer's goal
panels.caption: The outer pipeline sees whether the incentives produced efficient or wasteful outcomes.

panels.title: 5. Update the rules
panels.caption: The rule designer improves because the equilibrium block makes the consequence of each rule choice visible during training.

steps.text: The system receives the details of one problem instance, such as available actions, costs, or contract options, so it can design rules for that setting.
A trainable outer module picks rule settings that should steer the players toward a preferred outcome.
The equilibrium block computes the stable player response under those incentives because the final outcome depends on how players react, not only on what the designer intended.
The pipeline scores the resulting allocation, schedule, or contract outcome against the design goal.
The designer updates its rule choice because solved game instances reveal which rules create higher-value equilibria.

paras: The paper changes incentive design from hand-crafted problem-specific procedures into one trainable framework that can solve many equilibrium-based tasks with the same outer design logic.
object.object: the incentive rule that shapes player behavior

hidden.name: how a rule choice shifts the equilibrium outcome
paras: The main hidden quantity is the mapping from rule choice to equilibrium behavior. You can inspect the rule itself, but that does not reveal how several self-interested players will finally settle. Small rule changes may cause large shifts in the stable outcome because every player is reacting to every other player too.

The equilibrium block exposes that hidden mapping by computing the stable response inside the learning loop. That helps because the outer designer can then ask not just which rules look reasonable, but which rules actually induce the desired behavior.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark the hidden parts of the rule-to-outcome map that matter most for good incentive design.

reads.html: The hidden quantity is what players will actually do after seeing the designed rules, because the rule is only useful if it changes their settled behavior in the desired way.
The method makes equilibrium response part of a trainable pipeline so incentive rules can be optimized against the behavior they induce.

mechanism.h2: Why an internal equilibrium solver helps
paras: Without an internal equilibrium solver, incentive design becomes guesswork or repeated black-box search. You can try many rules and observe outcomes, but the outer learner has no structured way to connect one rule change to one outcome change. By putting the equilibrium computation inside the pipeline, the designer sees the consequence of a rule choice immediately in terms of player behavior and final outcome quality.

The same structure can be reused across several tasks because many incentive problems share the same two-level shape. There is always a designer choosing rules and players responding to those rules. That common shape lets one pipeline handle contract design, machine scheduling, and inverse equilibrium problems because only the game context changes while the outer logic of rule design stays the same.

math.h2: Choose incentives for the equilibrium they create
math.words: A compact summary is to pick the incentive rule that gives the best final outcome after the players settle on their equilibrium response under that rule.
symbols: overall value of one incentive rule choice
the stable player behavior produced by that rule in one problem instance
how good the resulting allocation, contract, or schedule is for the designer's goal
cost or penalty for using that incentive rule, such as wasted reward or poor fairness

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Rule A offers a strong bonus for early completion.
Under that rule, players settle on a schedule with outcome value 9 and rule cost 3.
Rule B offers a smaller bonus and yields outcome value 7 with rule cost 1.
Rule A scores 6, while Rule B also scores 6.
If a third rule reaches outcome value 8 with rule cost 1, it wins because it creates almost the same behavior with less wasted reward.

math.note: The paper's actual implementation uses equilibrium blocks inside a trainable pipeline, but this equation captures the central idea: judge a rule by the equilibrium it causes, not by the rule alone.

charts.title: Task-specific hand design or weak search
charts.note: Problem-specific procedures struggle to reuse knowledge because each new setting needs fresh equilibrium reasoning.

charts.title: Deep incentive design
charts.note: The paper reports one unified pipeline across several incentive tasks because the equilibrium block lets the same outer design logic operate on different games.

items.b: Some games have several plausible equilibria.
items.html: If more than one stable outcome exists, the designed rule may not lead to one predictable behavior, so the outer learner can receive noisy or ambiguous feedback.
The equilibrium block reduces the design burden, but very large games can still be expensive because the system must solve a difficult response problem inside each training step.

items.b: A good training sample mix may hide bad edge cases.
items.html: One pipeline can work well across many sampled instances and still fail on rare cases because those cases may push players into a different stable pattern.
The framework is strongest when the equilibrium solver is reliable and the design goal is well specified, because then the outer learner can improve rules from clear outcome feedback.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small two-player or three-player game family with context-dependent costs. Let an outer module choose one rule setting, such as a price, bonus, or contract term. For each context, solve the resulting stable player behavior and record the designer's final score. Compare a trainable design loop against a fixed rule baseline.

The demo should show that the learned rule changes across contexts because different games need different incentives. It should also show that solving the response pattern inside the loop improves final outcomes because the designer is reacting to actual player behavior, not only to surface rule descriptions.
demo.closing: A convincing demo must prove that incentive design gets better when the system can train through the equilibrium step, because desirable outcomes depend on how players respond to the chosen rules.
